Sampling Analog Signals on an STM32F4: From Polling to Timer-Driven Acquisition

A practical investigation of ADC conversion timing, interrupts, GPIO instrumentation and hardware-triggered sampling using STM32CubeIDE.

Reading a sensor is not just a matter of converting voltage into a number. The acquisition architecture determines when measurements are taken, how much CPU time is consumed and how repeatable the sampling interval is. In this laboratory, we compared three ways of acquiring a potentiometer signal with an STM32F4: software polling, end-of-conversion interrupts and periodic triggering from TIM2.

Engineering objective

Configure a 12-bit ADC, measure its actual conversion timing on an oscilloscope, transmit values through UART and then decouple the acquisition rate from the ADC's maximum conversion speed using a hardware timer.

12-bitADC resolution
15 MHzADC clock
1–2 HzTimer-driven sampling

Bringing up the measurement chain

USART1 was first configured on PA9/PA10 for asynchronous communication at 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and one stop bit. A blocking HAL_UART_Transmit() call sent a test message to Tera Term, establishing a simple diagnostic path before working with the ADC.

The potentiometer output was then connected to ADC3 channel 5 (PF7). The microcontroller ran at 180 MHz, while the APB2 peripheral clock was configured at 90 MHz. ADC3 used a 12-bit resolution and initially a 480-cycle sampling interval. GPIO PG13, connected to an on-board LED, served as an oscilloscope-visible timing marker.

ADC clock prescaler

The ADC clock follows the peripheral clock after prescaling:

fADC = fAPB2 / P

With fAPB2 = 90 MHz and P = 6, the resulting ADC clock is 15 MHz.

Predicting the conversion time

An STM32F4 successive-approximation ADC needs time to acquire the analog input on its sampling capacitor and additional clock cycles to resolve the digital code. For a 12-bit conversion, the STM32F4 timing model used here includes 12 conversion cycles after the configured sampling interval.

ADC conversion timing
tconv = (Nsample + 12) / fADC
fconv,max = fADC / (Nsample + 12)

At 480 sampling cycles: tconv = 492 / 15 MHz = 32.8 µs, corresponding to fconv,max ≈ 30.49 kHz before software overhead.

This is the conversion throughput limit under the selected settings, not automatically the rate at which a program records samples. Software execution, UART output and external triggers can make the actual acquisition rate lower.

Polling: straightforward, but blocking

In polling mode, the firmware starts an ADC conversion, waits for completion using HAL_ADC_PollForConversion(), and reads the result with HAL_ADC_GetValue(). The LED timing signal is set high before the wait and low after it, allowing the elapsed time to be inspected on the oscilloscope.

The report records a pulse width of approximately 33 µs, consistent with the theoretical 32.8 µs conversion duration. Its original text also mentions 30 µs in one reciprocal calculation; the 33 µs observation and the 30.49 kHz theoretical prediction are the mutually consistent values.

The ADC returned integer codes between 0 and 4095, as expected for 12-bit resolution. Varying the potentiometer changed the values seen in the debugger, and the same codes were formatted and transmitted over USART1.

Quantization of a 12-bit ADC
Ncodes = 212 = 4096
VLSB ≈ VREF / 4096

The ADC maps its reference-voltage span to 4096 quantization levels. The report demonstrates the digital range but does not specify a measured reference voltage, so no numerical LSB voltage is asserted.

Interrupts: reacting when a conversion completes

The next implementation enabled continuous conversion and the ADC interrupt in the NVIC. Rather than repeatedly waiting inside the main loop, firmware starts acquisition with HAL_ADC_Start_IT(). The end-of-conversion callback retrieves the new sample and changes the PG13 state.

Because the callback toggles PG13 once per conversion, a full square-wave period represents two conversions. The measured GPIO frequency must therefore be doubled to estimate the conversion rate:

GPIO toggle interpretation
fsample ≈ 2 fGPIO

A GPIO waveform near 15 kHz indicates approximately 30 ksample/s, consistent with the 480-cycle ADC setting.

Reducing the sampling interval to 28 cycles gives a theoretical throughput of 15 MHz / (28 + 12) = 375 ksample/s. The oscilloscope trace reports approximately 187.27 kHz at PG13, implying around 374.5 ksample/s after accounting for the toggle factor.

The choice of sampling time is also an analog design constraint: an excessively short acquisition window can degrade accuracy if the source impedance and ADC input sampling capacitance prevent proper settling.

Timer-triggered conversion: controlling when samples are taken

Fast continuous conversion is not always appropriate for slow-moving sensors. TIM2 was therefore configured to generate periodic update events, with ADC3 set to start a conversion from TIM2 TRGO rather than running continuously. The ADC interrupt still handles the completed sample; the timer determines when each conversion starts.

STM32 timer update frequency
fupdate = fTIM2 / [(PSC + 1)(ARR + 1)]

Here, PSC is the programmed prescaler register and ARR the auto-reload register. Their register values appear with +1 in the frequency equation. With a 90 MHz timer clock, the required divisor is 45,000,000 for 2 Hz or 90,000,000 for 1 Hz.

The first timer configuration generated a 2 Hz update rate because the required 1 Hz interval was initially misinterpreted. The original oscilloscope capture confirms this 2 Hz sampling configuration.

Configuration correction in the laboratory

The report explains that the supplied project was subsequently corrected for 1 Hz sampling. Its final screenshot shows a prescaler register value of 29,999 and a counter period of 2,999, giving (29,999 + 1) × (2,999 + 1) = 90,000,000 and thus 1 Hz at a 90 MHz timer clock. The authors observed an LED transition each second but did not have an oscilloscope available to repeat the precise measurement for that final configuration.

What the comparison demonstrates

Polling is simple and useful for bring-up, but keeps the CPU waiting. Interrupt-driven conversion lets firmware respond to completed measurements without polling the ADC status. Timer-triggered conversion makes the sample schedule depend on a hardware time base, a better fit when sensor data must be collected at controlled intervals.

All three methods were implemented and investigated on the STM32F4. The timing measurements support the theoretical ADC model, while the 1 Hz final configuration is supported by the firmware settings and LED observation rather than a final oscilloscope trace.

Engineering takeaway

The ADC's conversion speed and the application's sampling frequency are different design parameters. A robust acquisition chain must account for analog settling, peripheral clocks, CPU involvement, timing instrumentation and the system's actual data-rate requirements.
